items.title: New economic data challenges Fed chief’s not-too-hot perspective By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - New data may challenge Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh’s sense that the US economy can handle a robust expansion without stoking inflation, as a key measure of price pressures jumped and strong consumer spending and business investment pushed growth further beyond the level most central bank officials see as sustainable. Warsh, speaking on Wednesday after the Fed decided to hold interest rates steady, said he did not think the economy was "too hot," and that he did not want "to throw sand in the gears" of an expansion that has been gaining steam on the back of investment in artificial intelligence and consumer spending that continues to grow despite tepid gains in income. The jump in third-quarter gross domestic product, announced on Thursday by the US Commerce Department, however, was even faster than anticipated, with output growing at a 3.4% annualized rate in the July-September period, consumer spending rising by a robust 3.8%, and investment in business equipment up a massive 20.9%. The pace may not continue. Consumer spending, for example, grew faster than income in the recent GDP report, a situation some economists said was unlikely to last, and Warsh said on Wednesday that a recent tightening in credit markets showed investors had become "more discerning in their capital allocations," a possible precursor to slower investment growth. But the data in hand still show an economy that so far has not slowed despite the outlook for tighter monetary policy, with strong demand now coinciding with broad-based inflation. Different measures of inflation’s breadth show anywhere from roughly 50% to nearly 60% of the items in the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, the gauge the Fed uses for its 2% inflation target, posting annual price increases of more than 3% in September — far above pre-COVID-19 norms for a measure Warsh said he sees as a good indicator of underlying inflation trends. Though the number of items above that 3% level fell slightly last month, Diane Swonk, chief economist at KPMG, said the details of the PCE report showed inflation was broadly persistent across the economy, particularly in service industries where Fed rate hikes may have less of an impact. The PCE Price Index rose 3.6% in September after a 3.4% rise in the previous month, pushing it further away from the recent low of 2.3% in March 2025, near the start of President Donald Trump’s second term in the White House. Swonk said that while she felt Fed policymakers should have raised rates this week, she understood the motivation to be patient because "they don’t want a recession for 3% to 4% inflation" if they could tackle the problem more slowly and keep the current expansion going, a goal Warsh himself laid out

items.title: PCE inflation report September 2026:
items.excerpt: The pace of price increases stepped up in September, keeping inflation well above the Federal Reserve's target, while the economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, according to Commerce Department reports Thursday. The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% for the month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6%. The monthly increase was the largest since March but in line with the Dow Jones consensus, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below. Excluding food and energy, the core PCE posted respective readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, in line with the consensus. While the Fed follows both measures closely, officials generally see the core reading as more indicative of longer-term inflation trends. While inflation continued to run ahead of the Fed's 2% target, the Commerce Department also reported that gross domestic product was strong in the third quarter. GDP increased at a seasonally adjusted annualized pace of 3.4%, better than the 3.1% estimate and well ahead of the 2.2% in the second quarter. Also, in September consumer spending proved resilient, climbing 0.5%, a bit below the forecast for a 0.6% gain, while personal income rose 0.2%, compared with the estimate for 0.3%. The reports come the day after the Fed voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in a range between 3.75%-4%. Despite elevated inflation readings, central bank officials insist they can afford to evaluate incoming data before deciding on their next move. ... September's price increases were driven largely by a surge in energy costs that economists fear could be spreading to other parts of the economy. Gasoline and other energy goods saw a 9.2% rise for the month while energy goods and services broadly jumped 5.4%. At the same time, services prices excluding energy and housing rose 0.4%, and housing costs increased 0.3%.

items.title: U.S. Inflation Accelerates to 3.7% as Gasoline Prices Jump | EconoTimes
items.excerpt: U.S. inflation accelerated in September as gasoline prices climbed, while research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York points to a separate tariff-related pressure on consumer-goods costs. The Consumer Price Index (CPI), reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), rose 0.6% from August on a seasonally adjusted basis and 3.7% over 12 months, up from 3.4% in August. Gasoline prices increased 9.1% during the month, and the gasoline index was 34.2% higher than a year earlier. Food at home fell 0.1% for the month and rose 1.8% over the year. The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) reported that its personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index advanced 0.5% in September and 3.6% from a year earlier. Excluding food and energy, the index rose 0.3% for the month and 3.1% over 12 months. Neither release calculated tariffs’ contribution to overall inflation; the BLS said gasoline contributed more than half of September’s monthly CPI increase. In the New York Fed researchers’ model, a one-point rise in the average tariff rate corresponds to an estimated 0.25% increase in consumer-goods prices after 12 months. The researchers found that most tariff costs passed through to U.S. import prices. The researchers said higher costs for imported inputs can feed into retail prices through U.S. producers.
